props.title: Woman of the Year

sections.content: **Woman of the Year** (1942) launched the legendary Spencer Tracy-Katharine Hepburn partnership, setting the template for battle-of-the-sexes romantic comedies. Hepburn plays Tess Harding, a sophisticated international affairs columnist who clashes and falls for sports writer Sam Craig (Tracy). The film crackles with their natural chemistry while tackling then-radical themes about career women and marriage. Director George Stevens masterfully balances sharp dialogue with physical comedy, especially in the famous final scene where Tess hilariously fails at basic kitchen tasks. The film established the "career woman needs domesticity" trope that would influence decades of rom-coms like **Working Girl** (1988) and **The Devil Wears Prada** (2006).

sections.content: The Tracy-Hepburn dynamic revolutionized how Hollywood portrayed romantic relationships. Their nine films together showcased an equality and mutual respect rare for the era. **Adam's Rib** (1949) continued themes from Woman of the Year, with the couple as opposing lawyers in a gender-focused case. **Desk Set** (1957) updated their chemistry for the computer age. Their off-screen relationship infused their performances with an authenticity that influenced countless screen couples, from **When Harry Met Sally** (1989) to **You've Got Mail** (1998). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Career Women in Film

Woman of the Year kicked off decades of films exploring professional women balancing career and romance. **His Girl Friday** (1940) had already featured Rosalind Russell as a crack reporter, but Hepburn's Tess Harding represented a new level of female achievement and independence. The film's somewhat regressive ending - suggesting career women need domesticity - would be challenged by later films like **9 to 5** (1980) and **Working Girl** (1988). Modern takes like **The Proposal** (2009) still grapple with these themes while trying to avoid outdated gender politics.
